maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1964-65 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: A message from His Excellency the Governor General transmitting estimates for the financial year ending March 31, 1965, was presented by Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance) and read by Mr. Speaker to the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1964-65 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few observations relating to the main estimates for 1964-65 now being tabled.
Budgetary expenditures provided for in the estimates for the new fiscal year commencing April 1, 1964, including amounts already authorized by continuing statutes as well as moneys parliament is being requested to appropriate, amount to $6,703,513,508. Parliament is also being asked to authorize the disbursement of moneys for loans, investments and advances (which add to the government's active assets), in a total amount of $108,897,000.
Not included in these totals, but set out in the estimates for information, is the forecast amount for old age security pension payments amounting to $882 million. These pension payments are separated from the budget figures and are payable out of the old age security fund to which is credited the taxes levied for this particular purpose.
To compare the main estimates for 196465 totalling $6,703.5 million with expenditures authorized by parliament to date for 196364, $6,619.1 million, would be misleading. The latter figure does not include the final supplementary estimates for the current fiscal year, and the former figure takes no account of the supplementary estimates for the new fiscal year. It is for this reason that a reasonably accurate comparison of total expenditures for the year commencing April 1, 1964 with those for the current and previous fiscal years must await the budget presentation.
It is also misleading to compare the main estimates for the coming fiscal year with the main estimates for the current year, unless one takes note of certain differences in presentation. I will point out these differences. For example, the public debt
charges, which are statutory are shown in 1964-65 at some $157 million more than the amount included in the main estimates for
1963-	64. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the increase anticipated in 1964-65 over the expected actual expenditure in 1963-64 is about $52 million. This indicates a serious underestimate in the amount presented to parliament in the 1963-64 estimates. The amount included in the new estimates is forecast on a more comprehensive basis in which the costs of new refunding and other issues are based on interest rates prevailing just before the estimates were printed.
There is also the manner of presentation of the defence estimates. The main estimates for 1963-64 do not include an additional amount of $44 million required in that year to meet increases in pay and allowances for the armed forces. This distorts the year to year comparison. Both operating and capital grants to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are included in the main estimates for 1963-64, but only the operating grants- which incidentally are increased by $7.4 million-are included in the main estimates for
1964-	65. The capital requirements for 1964-65 amounting to $14.3 million are included in the loans section for that year.
Some of the increases in statutory expenditures in 1964-65 should be noted. Hospital insurance costs continue to rise at a rate of close to 10 per cent a year. An additional amount of $35 million is being provided in 1964-65 for this purpose. Estimated contributions by the government under the Trans-Canada Highway Act are increased by 10 million. The statutory contribution by the government of Canada to the Canadian corporation for the 1967 world exhibition requires the provision of $17.9 million. This is a new item in 1964-65 to meet the expected federal share of the fair corporation budget costs in that year.
In dealing with the statutory area of expenditures I would like to draw the attention of the house to the fact that although the government has announced its intention of increasing the equalization payments to provinces, the amount shown in the main estimates for 1964-65 does not include such increase since it has not yet been enacted by parliament. This is in keeping with the practice of not anticipating in the estimates proposed legislative changes.

Estimates Tabled
Mr. Speaker, when I tabled the main and first supplementary estimates for 1963-64 last May 29, I stated that treasury board was examining, with the assistance and co-operation of the ministers concerned, the programs of each department of government. This special examination has been completed and formed a prelude to the customary treasury board review of departmental proposals for the coming fiscal year. Substantial cutbacks in many expenditure programs were achieved as a result of this examination. At the same time provision is being made in the estimates for 1964-65 for the cost of new programs and new functions, including the new Department of Industry, as well as for substantial increases in the amounts provided for external aid and for grants for the scholarship and research programs of the national research council and medical research council. It should be noted also that as a consequence of the review of defence outlays now being conducted by my colleague the Minister of National Defence, an amount of $15 million has been included in the estimates for the Department of Public Works resulting from the transfer of responsibility to that department for the northwest highway system and for the maintenance of facilities at Fort Churchill.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the house to an important change in the form of the estimates for 196465. This change relates to the number of items to be voted. In former years the estimates contained some 500 or more separate votes. The main estimates for 1964-65 contain
only 230 such items. This reduction has been accomplished by consolidating a large number of the items formerly in the votes section of the estimates, while at the same time preserving the same amount of information as in the past in the details section. This change is in keeping with the recommendations of the royal commission on government organization, and puts into effect the proposal which was made by the government to the standing committee on public accounts last December. This committee has reported favourably to the house on the proposal, and I am hopeful that the change will do much not only to facilitate discussion of the estimates in the house, but also to improve the quality of financial management in the public service.
With the permission of the house, Mr. Speaker, I now propose to table for inclusion in Hansard three tables relating to the 196465 estimates. The first table compares the 1964-65 estimates with the total budgetary estimates for several preceding years. The second table compares the statutory expenditures for 1964-65 with those of 1963-64. The third table indicates the changes in the main estimates between 1963-64 and 1964-65 by an examination of operating, capital and other costs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement which the Minister of Finance has just given to the house is, of course, of great interest to all hon. members. I have not yet had the opportunity of seeing the statement; therefore I do not propose to comment upon the various figures of which he has advised the house. However, I am a little intrigued by his preliminary statement that on March 29, 1963 he advised the House of Commons of his estimates for that year. If he did that, Mr. Speaker, he was certainly guilty of more legerdemain than I realized he was capable of when he presented his budget.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, we have had a series of figures given us this afternoon which of course will be reviewed and studied by all hon. members. As I caught the statement of the minister I think he said, although I could be in error here, that the total amount of his estimates for the coming year will be $6,703,515,000 odd. If that figure is correct I would simply make the comment in passing that the estimates which were tabled in this house by the minister on May 29, 1963 were $6,545 million and some odd hundreds of thousands of dollars. It is true that figures do not mean a great deal on an occasion such as this. The minister can bring in supplementary estimates and in the end, as was done last year, alter the balances by charging up bookkeeping entries which should not be charged up at all. However, on the figures presented by the minister this afternoon we have an amount of $6,545 million odd as of last year and $6,703 million odd as of this year; and that figure, Mr. Speaker, despite the massive sacrifices which have been made by the Minister of National Defence in reducing the defence expenditures for this year. All I can say is that he must feel something like Atlas who rolled the stone up the hill only to see it come down again on top of him. Actually I am not sure whether this applies to the Minister of National Defence or the Minister of Finance, but one or the other must feel very badly crushed this afternoon.
In any event, I know this matter is not debatable, so I simply make this passing comment as a matter of fact and not as a matter of debate; we will have ample opportunity to study these figures as they are now presented to us. I have a sure feeling that you are going to have many opportunities to hear these matters debated in the days to come.

maintopic: BARLEY-ANNOUNCEMENT OP SALE TO RED CHINA

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: BARLEY-ANNOUNCEMENT OP SALE TO RED CHINA
speechtext:
I should like to inform the house that the Canadian wheat board announced in Winnipeg today that it has negotiated a contract for the sale of approximately 350,000 long tons of feed barley for shipment to mainland China. This sale, totalling approximately 16.3 million bushels, is for shipment from Vancouver during the period April through July 1964.
Payment for the barley is to be made on the basis of 25 per cent at the time of shipment with the remaining balance plus interest to be paid in 18 months. This credit arrangement is identical with the credit terms provided on the most recent wheat sale to China.
I know all members of the house will join me in expressing satisfaction with this additional sale of grain to mainland China by the wheat board.

maintopic: BARLEY-ANNOUNCEMENT OP SALE TO RED CHINA
speechtext: I think the house will be glad to hear this confirmation of the rumour that has been in the press this last two or three weeks about the barley sale. I hope this time the government in its conversations with the Canadian wheat board will reconsider the fact that they turned down Chinese wheat sales in December, to see if it would not be possible, with the new capacity created by co-operation out on the west coast, to fulfil the 18 million bushel wheat order that the Chinese would have liked to place last December.

maintopic: BARLEY-ANNOUNCEMENT OP SALE TO RED CHINA
speechtext: am sure the members of the house and particularly the prairie farmers will be delighted by the minister's announcement regarding this sale of barley to mainland China. I hope at some early opportunity the minister will make it clear whether the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, who is going to mainland China next week, is part of the deal.

maintopic: BARLEY-ANNOUNCEMENT OP SALE TO RED CHINA
speechtext:
I join with other members of the house in welcoming the announcement that has just been made. I think perhaps we could have some discussion and some more emphasis placed on expanding the facilities for loading this grain at the terminals on the west coast and take care of this additional sale, along with the other commitments that we have to deliver through the west coast during this crop year.

On the orders of the day:

maintopic: BARLEY-ANNOUNCEMENT OP SALE TO RED CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question, in French, to the minister of trade.
Could the minister tell the house if, upon signing the latest long term agreement concluded with red China for the sale of Canadian wheat, Canada undertook to buy textile products from mainland China?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: BARLEY-ANNOUNCEMENT OP SALE TO RED CHINA
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. In the last transaction between the Canadian wheat board and the China Resources Company it was agreed by the China Resources Company, acting on behalf of that country, that they would limit their exports to Canada. There is no undertaking on the part of Canada to buy anything from China.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CANADIAN HIGH SCHOOL PARTICIPATION IN CAMPAIGN AGAINST YAWS
speechtext: Having noted a recent reference in the press to a developing program throughout Canadian high schools, the students' war against yaws, would the Minister of National Health and Welfare indicate her interest in project SWAY, as it is called, and the manner in which it is hoped this very interesting development may go forward?

speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CANADIAN HIGH SCHOOL PARTICIPATION IN CAMPAIGN AGAINST YAWS
speechtext:
The students' war against yaws, or project SWAY, was initiated by the students of Mount Royal high school in Mount Royal, Quebec, as their way of marking Canada's centennial year. High schools across Canada have been invited to participate in the campaign against this highly contagious, disfiguring tropical disease, and already an amount of $1,400 has been raised and turned over to the director general of the world health organization which is attempting to eradicate this disease. The executive board of WHO passed a special resolution commending the high school children of Canada for their unselfish interest in the health of people in other parts of the world.
More and more high schools across the country are indicating their willingness to participate in this campaign, and I understand that a further appeal will be going out from the Mount Royal students within the next month or so. My department will certainly do everything it can in support of this commendable effort.
Yaws is a disease which now affects more than four million persons, and another one

hundred million are exposed to it. Fortunately, though, it can be treated successfully with a dose of penicillin equivalent in cost to the price of an ice cream sundae.
I support most enthusiastically the campaign of the Canadian high school students and look forward to an increasing measure of success in their further efforts.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs) moved:
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
That the treaty between Canada and the United States of America relating to co-operative development of the water resources of the Columbia river basin, signed at Washington on January 17, 1961, together with the protocol containing modifications and clarifications to the treaty annexed to an exchange of notes between the governments of Canada and the United States signed on January 22, 1964, be referred to the standing committee on external affairs.
He said: There are problems and rewards which I am sure we all recognize, for those of us in public life. As to the latter of these, perhaps the most satisfying is the sense, on occasion, of having been able to participate in and contribute to the achievement of policies or programs that can have lasting values and benefits for our country.
Columbia River Treaty
Today it is my privilege to invite all members of this house to share with me in this sense of participation and contribution. We have before us for our attention today, documents that comprise arrangements that will stand in history as a truly great accomplishment in the co-operation of two nations. There is no shadow of doubt, or hesitation in my mind when I say that I believe they represent a high point in the combination of legal, technical, and economic sciences for the advantage of both Canada and the United States, and when I say Canada, of course that includes the owner of the resource in Canada, the province of British Columbia.
So it is with real and deep pleasure that I bring the Columbia river treaty and protocol before this house for its consideration. The treaty was negotiated and signed by a previous government of Canada and the previous government of the United States. The protocol and the covering exchange of notes were negotiated and signed by the present government of Canada and the present government of the United States. These documents represent the best efforts of successive governments in both countries and reflect the wishes of the province where the Columbia river is located.
There has been much public discussion of the treaty, the protocol that has been negotiated in recent months to modify and clarify it, and the arrangements that are ancillary to these documents. It is difficult to deal with them without fear of restating things that are known or stressing what might have become obvious. However, it is equally clear from many comments that have been made that there is still a very great amount of misunderstanding and misinformation about the nature of the agreement. This is not surprising, since it is a very complicated question. It is doubtful if this parliament has had before it a document involving more complexities and technicalities. That being so, and recognizing the importance of this project, I trust that the house will bear with me while I try to set forth in broad terms what it is that the treaty and protocol are drawn to do. I shall not attempt to go into detail; that is something that I believe should be left for the work of the committee on external affairs. My statement, however, will be comprehensive because of the importance of the matter which is now before us.
Before going into the treaty itself, I should mention briefly the procedure that the government is proposing. It has been understood for some time that the treaty and now of course the protocol which is an essential part of it would be referred to the committee on external affairs. In addition, the committee will have available for examination other

Columbia River Treaty relevant papers, such as the supplementary agreement with the province of British Columbia, and the exchange of notes with the United States to which is appended an attachment relating to the terms of sale of downstream benefits. These documents are part of the information which the committee will no doubt be taking into account in its formal action on the treaty and the protocol. All of this and other documentary material has been assembled for the convenience of the house and the committee in the white paper which was tabled and distributed to this house yesterday.
The government will present to the committee a thorough analysis of the treaty and related documents, when the committee meets, and will provide expert evidence on all points at that time. The committee in turn will undoubtedly want to invite interested parties to present their views.
When consideration by the committee has been completed, the government will recommend to parliament the passage of a resolution approving the treaty and protocol. When that resolution is passed the government will be in a position to exchange instruments of ratification with the United States. It is expected that that will take place on or about October 1, 1964. Approval by this house, however, is needed at the earliest possible date in order that engineering, financial and administrative arrangements for the great work can proceed without delay.
Now, sir, the Columbia is one of the great rivers of the world. In North America its length and average volume of run-off are exceeded only by the Mississippi, the Mackenzie and the St. Lawrence. No river in North America exceeds it in energy potential: it is substantially the greatest river of them all.
The Columbia river and its tributaries drain an area of 259,000 square miles, the largest part of it in the United States. The sources of the Columbia itself and one of its major tributaries, the Kootenay, are in Canada. After rising in Columbia lake the Columbia river flows north and then at its great bend turns south through a total length of 480 miles in Canada. In the United States it flows a further 745 miles to the sea. In the course of that trip the waters of the Columbia river fall just over half a mile, to be exact 2,655 feet. It is that enormous drop combined with the great volume of water carried by the Columbia, the Kootenay, the Pend d'Oreille and tributaries in the United States that provide the tremendous energy potential.
Up until now there has not been one single installation on the main stem of the Columbia

river in Canada to provide either storage or the production of electric energy. In part, that fact is a reflection of the major character of the river. The requirements of British Columbia have until now been such that the great costs of harnessing this river have not been justified. The only installations to produce power on the entire system in Canada are on the lower reaches of the major tributaries, the Kootenay and the Pend d'Oreille rivers, just before they join the Columbia river, and on some of the minor tributaries.
In the United States the situation is quite different. Some of the largest storages and hydroelectric plants in North America have been installed. Power installations completed or under construction on the main stem of the Columbia now total approximately 10 million kilowatts of capacity. On the tributaries more than 5 million kilowatts have been installed. These totals are, however, only about half the potential of the system in the United States, which is estimated at 35 million kilowatts of installed capacity.
To give some idea of the magnitude of such a potential, it can be compared with the total present installed hydroelectric capacity of all Canada, which is just over 20 million kilowatts. In other words the Columbia system in the United States alone has a capacity 75 per cent greater than all our presently developed hydro in Canada; this fact is not without significance to the situation and in the course of our discussion and study of the treaty this will become increasingly clear.
To develop hydroelectric power effectively the water that falls through the turbines must be capable of control. Its flow should be controlled so that it passes through in just the quantity wanted at just the time wanted. As hon. members know, consumption of electric power varies enormously at different hours of the day and at different seasons of the year. Consumption goes up when factories are in operation during the day, when meals are being cooked and when the bustle of life is going on. Consumption drops during the night.
Normally in this country consumption is highest during the winter months when the days are short and cold, when furnaces consume electric power and when other energy needs are greater than in the summer months. Unless the flow of water can be adjusted to these requirements, it is not possible to realize the maximum value of the potential of this or any other river. Unfortunately nature takes no account of human requirements in its provision of water. In the case of some rivers such as the St. Lawrence, nature has been reasonably co-operative. The difference between high and low flows is only of the order of about two to one. This small seasonal

variation greatly minimizes the control needed to adjust the flow reasonably well to human needs.
In the case of the Columbia, nature could hardly have been less co-operative. The highest flows come in the summer v/hen the needs are least, and the lowest flows are in the winter when the needs are greatest. In addition, the variation of flow is fantastic. At the international boundary the extremes of flow have gone from an estimated high of 680,000 cubic feet per second to an estimated low of 12,900 cubic feet per second, a ratio of approximately 50 to 1. At Revelstoke further up the Columbia, the highest recorded flow is 99 times greater than the lowest.
It is not surprising that with these enormous variations the Columbia is not only extremely difficult to harness for electric power but is also, without maximum control, a great danger to the people living near it. We will recall that as recently, as 1948, a flood killed 50 people, left 38,000 homeless and destroyed a community in the United States numbering 18,000 persons. From these characteristics arise both the problems and the opportunities in developing the Columbia river.
I have referred to the installations on the United States section of the Columbia river. Some of the great power and reclamation projects of the world are there, such as Grand Coulee, Hungry Horse, John Day and Chief Joseph. The United States has already invested some $3 billion in these projects. However, because of the enormous variations in flow these installations cannot produce their full power potential. They require more storage than now exists on the river and its tributaries. For the development of the full potential there must be enough storage to level out the flows and change them from the fantastic feast and famine of nature into the controlled flows demanded by human requirements. If such control can be provided, not only will the production of electric power be enormously increased but the means will at the same time have been provided to eliminate a great flood danger.
There were two ways in which this problem could be approached. One would have been for Canada and the United States independently to develop their own part of the Columbia entirely for their own purposes and without regard to development on the other side of the boundary. Canada could have adopted this course. It would, however, have meant the construction of very costly storage dam sites and generating plants lower down in Canada. The result would have been expensive power in the early stages of development, so expensive that two engineer-
Columbia River Treaty ing firms have questioned whether development would be worth while at all.
At the same time that this expensive power was being produced in Canada, Canadian storages would have given the United States automatically, without any undertaking or obligation of the United States to make payment for it, a good deal of the regulation that they wanted, but not as efficiently as if it were planned jointly. Similarly, for the United States to go it alone would have meant the construction of storages of their own at costs much greater than for similar storages in Canada.

speechtext: And flooded a lot of their own land.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext: Pardon?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
And flood a lot of their
own land, which they are thankful not to have to do.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
The common sense course obviously was to evaluate the advantages of working together, and to explore the possibilities of undertaking developments on a planned, co-operative basis. To get this appraisal, a reference was made to the international joint commission by the governments of Canada and the United States in March, 1944.
It was not possible for these studies to proceed actively during the war years or immediately thereafter. Studies of this kind are enormously difficult and, as my hon. friend from Kootenay West knows, very complicated. As a result, it was not until 1959 that the international Columbia river engineering board submitted its report to the international joint commission.
An abstract of the report is set out in the white paper which I tabled yesterday, and I would particularly draw attention to the following comments that set forth the findings based on many years of careful investigation. First of all, at page 26:
The water resources of the Columbia river basin can be developed for a variety of purposes. Maximum utilization of these resources can be achieved only by implementation of a comprehensive plan of development covering all parts of the basin.
Then, on the same page, the report goes on to point out:
The largest and most valuable tangible use of the water resources of the basin, either existing or in the foreseeable future, is for hydroelectric power production. Therefore, the full development of the hydroelectric power potential has been a primary goal.
And at page 27:
It is evident that if the goal of maximum hydroelectric power development can be attained, flood control will be assured, and it should be possible to develop all other water uses.

Columbia River Treaty
Then the board makes the following conclusions, as shown on page 37:
(k)	Three possible methods of developing the Kootenay and upper Columbia rivers produce potential benefits nearly equal in terms of total effect in the basin...In view of these factors, and having regard to the practical limits of accuracy of the studies, no one plan of development can be selected as representing the optimum use of sites and water resources.
Then at page 38:
(l)	The method of co-operative development of the Kootenay and upper Columbia rivers will be determined by considerations beyond the scope of this report, but the information provided herein on the alternative plans will provide a reasonable basis for discussion between the two countries.
And on the same page:
(p) For any further progress towards co-operative development, some measure of general agreement between the two countries should be reached with respect to principles for sharing benefits and costs. Project justification requires the use of such principles to determine the benefits and costs to be ascribed to individual components of an agreed plan of development.
Now, Mr. Speaker, these conclusions which were caused to be made by a body set up by another administration, a body composed of men of great technical competence, are very basic to the presentation which is inherent in the treaty signed by the right hon. gentleman opposite, and the protocol which was recently signed in Washington, in January of this year.
Thus in 1959 the two governments had answers to their main questions of 1944. Cooperative development of the water resources of the Columbia river basin would be practical and in the public interest. That is the conclusion. They also had the definite indication that further progress would require agreement on the way in which benefits and costs could be shared.
The governments of the day of both countries next directed the international joint commission to recommend the principles called for in the conclusions which I have just read to the house, principles that should be applied in determining the benefits that would be derived from co-operative development and the apportionment between the two countries of such benefits, more particularly in relation to electric generation and flood control.
This direction was given in January, 1959, and in December of the same year the international joint commission made its report. That report is set out, beginning on page 39 of the white paper tabled yesterday, and I would particularly draw hon. members' attention to the following salient principles: Power principle No. 6.
The power benefits determined to result in the downstream country from regulation of flow by

storage in the upstream country should be shared on a basis such that the benefit, in power, to each country will be substantially equal, provided that such sharing would result in an advantage to each country as compared with alternatives available to that country.
Flood control principle No. 4.
The upstream country should be paid one half of the benefits as measured in flood control principle No. 3, i.e., one half of the value of the damages prevented.
Now, sir, at this point I would like to pay my tribute to the members of the international joint commission for their far reaching achievement in arriving at a set of principles of such significance. Above all, credit must be given to the then chairman of the Canadian section, General McNaughton, who had the wisdom, the foresight and the determination to achieve agreement on a body of principles that were basic to participation by Canada in a co-operative system of development. The principles were not, of course, binding on the two governments, nor did they go into any of the problems of specific application. They were, however, of great importance. As the then prime minister, the present Leader of the Opposition, said in a statement on December 30, 1959:
They would be of great value to the governments concerned in the negotiations which lie ahead.
At that point the stage had been set for the beginning of actual negotiations. On January 25, 1960, the then prime minister, the right hon. gentleman who presently leads the opposition, announced that negotiations would open on the following February 11. The operation that then began, and continued through until mid-January, 1961, was probably as complex and arduous a process of negotiation, co-ordination and consultation as has ever been undertaken in Canada.
While the negotiations with the United States were the responsibility of the government of Canada, it was obvious that the province of British Columbia, the owner of the Canadian water resources in question, had to be immediately and continuously involved at every step. In order to ensure that there would be full co-ordination, a federal-provincial policy liaison committee had been set up. Its membership was impressive. It included both federal and provincial ministers, the entire negotiating team, General McNaughton, legal, technical and economic advisers. That group had eight sessions of meetings in the course of 1960.
There was in addition a technical liaison committee which included federal and provincial engineers, economists and other technical experts. That committee carried out

specific investigations as required by the policy liaison committee, and advised it constantly.
The negotiating team representing Canada included not only the tour members announced by the then prime minister on January 25, 1960, but also a large supporting team of experts, and these were drawn not only from the federal and provincial governments themselves but also from the Canadian section of the international joint commission and, from time to time, included outside technical advisers on specific points.
Within the government itself a cabinet committee was established consisting of ministers most directly concerned to keep the whole development constantly under review and to consider all matters of policy.
The negotiating team held eight meetings in the course of 1960 and a ninth in January of 1961, resulting in the Columbia river treaty. That treaty was signed on January 17 of that year by the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), the then minister of justice, Hon. E. D. Fulton, and our ambassador in Washington, Mr. Arnold Heeney, on behalf of Canada. For the United States, it was signed by President Eisenhower, the secretary of state of the United States, Mr. Herter, and the head of their negotiating team, the then under secretary of the interior, Mr. Elmer Bennett.
At this point I should like to pay my own tribute to what was done by the former government, the government of that day, as well as by all those who were involved in this arduous operation. It reflects great credit on all concerned. Not only were the complex and infinitely trying negotiations pursued vigorously but, I have been told by many who were involved, Mr. Davie Fulton led the Canadian side with distinction from beginning to end. The treaty moved ahead to prompt approval in the United States where it passed the Senate on March 16, 1961. In Canada, however, differences developed between the federal and provincial governments. I think there is no purpose to be served in going back over the details of what these were or how they arose. In part, they were related to plans by the provincial government for development of the Peace river and to differences of view as to the priority that should be accorded to that development in relation to the Columbia river project. Whatever the source or the merit of the differences of view, one question that does occur is whether the situation could not have been avoided by ensuring that there was, in fact and beyond doubt, clear agreement with British Columbia before the treaty was signed.
Columbia River Treaty
Commenting on the situation in an address in Vancouver on October 2, 1961, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) said:
The time has long since gone by when a federal government should sign an agreement with the U.S.A. or any other country which requires provincial action and co-operation for its implementation, without a clear and formal undertaking from the province concerned that the terms of the agreement are such that this co-operation will be forthcoming.
The Prime Minister went on to refer to the "kind of co-operation and action which was signed, sealed and delivered" between Ontario and the federal government before the St. Lawrence agreement with the U.S.A. was concluded.
Fortunately the differences of view did not impose any delay on the engineering work which had to be carried out to provide accurate and detailed information for the storage dams that the treaty contemplated. That work went ahead actively and with no loss of time. Several meetings and discussions between representatives of the federal and provincial governments occurred in 1961 and
1962.	In the latter part of 1962 there were also meetings at the official level with the United States to discuss possible terms for the sale of Canadian downstream power benefits in the United States for a period of years. The situation was, however, still unresolved when the present government assumed office in April 1963.
One of the tasks to which highest priority was given by the government was the determination of the action that should be taken to meet some of the criticisms that had developed about the treaty provisions. The essential question was whether it was desirable and practical to try to negotiate a new treaty, or whether it would be preferable to build on the foundation that had been laid. I have no hesitation in saying, Mr. Speaker, that the more I studied the treaty and the complex situation with which it was designed to deal, the more I became impressed by the achievement which it represented. I concluded that what we had to do was to make a basically good treaty better still. That, I am confident, we have done.
The first step was taken by the Prime Minister in his meeting with the late president of the United States at Hyannis Port in May
1963.	The Prime Minister and the president there agreed to initiate negotiations on a protocol which would embody clarification and adjustments in certain of the treaty arrangements.
Before negotiation with the United States could proceed, the present government felt that agreement with British Columbia was imperative. We could not have a treaty without agreement with British Columbia. I have

Meetings to achieve the kind of agreement the Prime Minister referred to were undertaken last June and July and resulted in the signature of an agreement on July 8, 1963. That agreement is set forth at page 100 of the white paper. It was subsequently supplemented by a further agreement of January 13 of this year and in those two documents there is a clear statement of the rights, obligations and relationships of the two governments in every aspect that is involved in the treaty, the protocol and the arrangements that will arise under them. Incidentally, although the previous government had offered to assist the province of British Columbia by meeting half the costs of the whole development, the arrangements which have now been made do not involve any financial contribution whatsoever by the federal government. In fact, paragraph 12(3) of the agreement of July 8 states specifically that "Canada shall have no obligation for the financing of these treaty projects". This accords fully with the objectives outlined by the Prime Minister in October, 1961 when he said:
We must establish in advance of ratification the export price of energy, not leave it to be negotiated afterwards. I do not see any advantage in using public funds to build power and storage dams merely for the purpose of making electrical energy available at exceptionally low rates in the United States.
Having achieved agreement within our borders between the owner of the resource and the Canadian government, it was possible to proceed with negotiations with the United States. These began on August 1, 1963 and carried on through a series of meetings and, at times, difficult negotiating sessions which arrived at a successful conclusion in agreement on a protocol. The protocol is attached to an exchange of notes that were signed by myself, as Secretary of State for External Affairs, and the Secretary of State of the United States on January 22, in the presence of the Prime Minister and President Johnson.

The main feature of the original treaty is its provision for construction of the dams in Canada at Arrow lakes, Duncan lake and Mica creek that will provide a very large amount of storage. No one knows it better than my hon. friend, whose interruptions help me along as I go from point to point. Part, though by no means all, of the storage will be committed for operation on agreed terms to produce power benefits in the United States which will be shared equally between the two countries, as well as substantial power benefits in and for Canada itself. Some of this storage will also be operated to provide flood control, and substantial payment will be made to Canada for flood damage prevented in the United States. The treaty contemplated in article VIII that downstream power benefits, if not brought back to Canada, might be sold in the United States on agreed terms.
The treaty also allows for the construction by the United States of a dam on the Kootenay river, near Libby, Montana, the reservoir of which will extend some 40 miles into Canada. The United States will pay the entire cost of that dam. All Canada provides is the relatively small amount of land that will be flooded on our side of the boundary. For that very small contribution Canada gets major benefits in flood control and increased power production after the river re-enters Canada. Those benefits are not subject to any sharing with the United States.
The treaty contains provisions regarding permissible diversions, the designation of operating entities, the establishment of a joint permanent engineering board, procedures for settling differences, provisions for restoring the pre-treaty legal position after the treaty has been terminated, and limitations on liability for damages.

Paragraph 3 of the protocol provides that an exchange of notes that is to arrange for a sale of power shall take place at the same time as the exchange of the instruments of ratification. As I shall describe in a moment, the terms of sale have in fact been worked out. As a result, we now know in advance of ratification precisely how much money the sale will yield and just how that yield will compare with the costs that Canada incurs under the treaty. I believe that that represents a very essential and important improvement over the treaty signed in 1961.
Three of the paragraphs of the protocol deal with flood control.
Paragraph 1 meets a criticism that had been levied that Canada would not have an adequate voice in determining whether flood control operation is needed in circumstances of special emergency over and above the basic flood control provisions of the treaty. In effect, the situation is that Canada is paid in advance a very large amount of money-$64.4 million in U.S. funds-for what is called "primary flood control" operation. There is a further provision that enables the United States to call for additional flood control in certain circumstances, and it had been felt that there was no adequate protection against misuse of that provision.
Paragraph 1 of the protocol requires that the United States entity requesting the additional flood control must submit its requests to the Canadian operating entity. The latter can accept, reject or suggest modifications to these requests. If agreement between the entities cannot be reached, the request is then submitted to the permanent engineering board, a joint Canada-United States body. The board's decision will be binding on both entities. If, however, the board fails to agree as to the need for the flood control, the request must be honoured so that the possibility of loss of life and damage to property will be minimized. The provision under the treaty by which Canada is reimbursed for loss incurred through such flood control operation continues in effect.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the protocol is also quite specific as to when the United States can call for additional flood control. It not only specifies the degree of flood for which flood control protection will be provided, but requires that all United States storage in the basin be employed first before calls are made on additional Canadian storage.
Paragraph 2 of the protocol inserts a specific requirement that any operating plans for flood control to be carried out under the treaty and protocol must be prepared in a manner which will minimize flood damage in both the United States and Canada. While substantial flood.

control protection to Canada is automatic when the treaty projects are in operation, the specific inclusion of Canadian needs in the determination of flood control plans was not provided for in the treaty. This is an important clarification of that document.
Finally, sir, on the subject of flood control, paragraph 11 allows for the upward adjustment of the payments to Canada for flood control protection in the event that treaty storages are completed earlier than is called for by the treaty. This adjustment will be calculated on the same basis as the treaty payments.
I have dealt so far with the substantial improvements provided by the protocol in relation to the primary benefits that are to be produced and shared under this cooperative development project: the power benefits and the flood control benefits. A concern in the negotiation of the treaty was to ensure that, while securing these benefits, there should be no more limitation than was absolutely necessary on Canada's freedom to use the waters to meet other Canadian needs. In this connection, doubt had been expressed as to whether Canadian rights of diversion had been adequately protected. The protocol goes further than the treaty in ensuring these rights.

I should like to state briefly, Mr. Speaker, a few objective points in favour of this bill.


At this point, Mr. Speaker, I would like to summarize some of the main factors behind the introduction of Bill No. C-2. First, the name Air Canada is certainly bilingual. It has precisely the same connotation and meaning in English and in French, the two official languages of our nation.
The name Air Canada is a shorter appellation which does away with cumbersome translation, as is the case with Trans-Canada Air Lines, which in French is Les Lignes Aerien-nes Trans-Canada.
Many countries of the world are already using a designation of this kind to identify their national air lines. This is the case with Air India, Air France, Air Liban, Air Algerie and Swissair, to name but a few. Originally the name Trans-Canada Air Lines served to designate an air line which serviced a domestic network of communications. This designation is no longer acceptable because the air line now services routes that go beyond the nation's geographical frontiers, indeed routes that touch many parts of the world.
In certain airports in the United States travellers tend to be confused because two separate air lines use the initials T.C.A. One is Trans-Canada Air Lines, and the other is Trans-Caribbean Air Lines.
Another bill, similar in nature and substance, was introduced in this house in 1961 by an hon. member from the province of Ontario-I am referring to the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) who has since been appointed Minister of National Health and Welfare.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw your attention to an editorial by Mr. Ayotte, published in La Presse on October 12, 1963, and which refers to an article published on the same subject in the Financial Post. It said in French:

"Even Toronto wants the designation Air Canada."
It is not only French Canada which is requesting that our state-owned air line should be designated only by the words Air Canada. The Financial Post of Toronto advocates it in terms much more pressing than those we used at any time we raised the question these last few years.
First of all, the editorial published in the great financial paper of Toronto is entitled as follows:
Be brave, Ottawa, be brave.
And it says, among other things:
The government and T.C.A. show a remarkable restraint in using the word "Air Canada", except in a limited way and in appropriate places.

But-adds the paper-why could the government not call this air service "Air Canada"? Why maintain a double wording that is unsatisfactory, confusing and quite unnecessary?
The Financial Post then observes that a French Canadian who would ask, a hundred miles away from his province, where is the nearest Air Canada office, would get the impression from the answer he would get that he is a stranger in his own country.
I should like to point out that those are the very words used in the editorial of the Financial Post.
Air France, Air Liban and Air Algerie are names which are understood throughout the world, and it would be the same thing with Air Canada. It would be much more simple and elegant than the long and complicated designation Trans-Canada Air Lines. Indeed, as has been pointed out, that name is no longer appropriate since the corporation's operations reach far beyond Canada.
We can therefore conclude with the influential Toronto weekly:
Air Canada would be a fine and prestigious designation in the world. Furthermore, it would indicate the bilingual character of our country, which is not an unimportant aspect.
Mr. Speaker, I have tried to be as objective as possible in presenting a few arguments in favour of the designation Air Canada.
I feel that that name is quite acceptable, that its use would be advantageous throughout the world and that, in Canada itself, it would correspond to the bicultural nature of the country, not to mention the fact that it would indicate the international character of Trans-Canada Air Lines, a corporation which in a few minutes time, I hope, will see its name changed to Air Canada.

speechtext:
I see the Solicitor General wants a few more minutes to make up his mind. This government which planned so carefully is not quite ready for this piece of legislation.
This is a very minor change to the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act. I understand the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Tremblay) spent most of last session as a sort of shadow behind the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays), and he was making himself informed on ARDA so I am sure he will be able to contribute to this debate that expert knowledge that an ordinary opposition member cannot supply. I will leave it to him to make comments on my proposed amendment from the viewpoint of its legality or propriety in relation to the act.
The reason this bill was introduced is to bring to the attention of the Indian affairs branch and the tribes or bands themselves the possibilities which exist under this act. If I may be allowed to make to the house and to the minister a point which everyone of us has discovered about ARDA, I should like to say that the initiative, if we are to accomplish anything, has to come from the provinces. I know this has been a rather bitter discovery in Ontario to many of us when we have realized that we have created this agency, have a good director and a wonderful piece of legislation, but yet have to mark time and wait for the provinces to come through. Some have done very well; others are dragging their feet. Ontario has just got into it recently. But the point is that this marvellous piece of legislation, which I think was the most inspired piece of legislation introduced by the previous government, requires some initiative on the part of the provinces. Indian affairs and band council affairs in the main have nothing to do with the provinces at all. They are a federal responsibility. But the fact remains that many of the reserves in Canada will fit within regional ARDA projects, or could in themselves be ARDA projects. I can give examples of this. I think of my neighbour in Fort William and of the Mission reserve where there could be all kinds of projects associated with ARDA projects, such as training the Indians in forestry and agricultural practices relating to the kind of land they have, and in equipping them to earn a better living, which is one of the key problems which the Indians have.
This is the reason why I introduced these amendments, because it would enable Indian

Agricultural Rehabilitation Act bands and the Indian branch, despite the fact that it is also another agency of the federal government like ARDA, officially to take the initiative and not have to wait for that provincial impetus that is required at the present time.
I know the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has been watching ARDA and will be aware how difficult it is to get projects going under ARDA without a strong lead from the province. What it really means, and what is developing in most places, is that to a great extent the local communities have to develop some kind of general idea through professional groups such as foresters groups and farm associations, and then it has to be promoted on the provincial political level in order to get the provincial ARDA people into the thing. It is a long cumbersome process and in the meantime, to my knowledge, I do not know of a single case where an Indian reserve or reserve lands has been vitally affected by the application of the act. And I think this is a pity.
I have had returns over a number of years to questions I have placed with regard to forest lands and agricultural lands in Indian reserves of Canada, and to say they are in good shape from either a forestry or agricultural point of view would be a lie. As a matter of fact, forestry management of many Indian lands is still in an embryo stage, and the fact remains that many of the people who live on Indian reserve lands are not capable at the present time of intelligent forestry management or agricultural management of their lands because they have never been fitted into the kind of project that ARDA provides. I know from knowledge of my own area what a dreadful thing it is that so many of the adult Indians today are living on welfare. They are living from ration to ration because they have lost so much of their incentive and drive. I am bitterly disappointed, and I know this is shared by many members in this house, at the failure of the Indian affairs department to come up with any program other than a long range educational program to improve the economic lot of the Indians in relation to their land. This is one more reason why I feel it would be important to pass this bill.
I know criticisms can be made of the bill from the point of view that it really is unnecessary, since it would be possible to develop these projects without the amendment. My point is it will be much easier to get the projects; it will put pressure upon the Indian affairs branch and upon the bands, if the amendments are made. For that reason I would like to suggest to the Solicitor General that this bill, or its subject matter could be referred very properly to the agriculture committee, and if it was done very soon we could get a report on it.

I understand that the minister-I have forgotten what his title is, but he is the minister for eastern agriculture and forestry and so on -is not going to take over ARDA for some weeks, until some kind of legislative changes have taken place. It is for this reason I would suggest this measure should go to the agriculture committee rather than to the committee on mines, forests and waters, and I would appreciate it if the Solicitor General and the ministry would consider this very seriously. At the very least, sending it to the committee would be in no way a stamp of approval for it. The committee could make up their minds, and I think many members would like the opportunity when the bill would be before the agriculture committee to have an examination of the progress that ARDA is making, particularly in its relation to the hinterland areas where Indian reserves are a potential for ARDA projects, but have not really had an opportunity or have really not been pushed as yet.
Mr. Ian Watson (Chateauguay-Huntingdon-
Laprairie): I, along with almost all members of the house, approve the principle of the bill introduced by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). The ARDA program is really the first approach that any government in Canada has ever made to the interrelated problems of agriculture, and the social problems resulting from the marginal areas of agriculture that are found in pockets throughout Canada, and to perhaps a greater extent the eastern part of the province of Quebec and the maritimes. I think this ARDA program is the first real hope that the people living in the marginal areas of agriculture have for improvement in their living standards.
The ARDA program combines a desire on the part of the Department of Agriculture to improve the agriculture in these marginal areas with a program which has its roots in the community affected. I believe the success of the ARDA program in any particular community is dependant upon the people living in that community. The local people must first come up with an idea, and present it to the Department of Agriculture which now administers ARDA. Later this idea, if it is approved, is developed in co-operation with the provinces into a federally financed self-help program. As far as the Indian reserves in Canada are concerned, the state of agriculture on almost all reserves in southern Canada has been at a low ebb since perhaps the turn of the century. For a period after the reserves were awarded to the various Indian tribes, a number of Indians were taught the skills of agriculture and settled down to fairly prosperous farming ventures. However, in the last 30 or 40 years, especially in southern Quebec

and Ontario, the Indians living on reserves have tended to drift away to work in the cities, and as a result agriculture on the reserves in southern Quebec and southern Ontario, has fallen into a complete state of disrepair.
The agricultural situation in the St. Regis and Caughnawaga reserves, which I represent, is best described as one where all the farms located on the reserves are weed-filled and growing over with brush, and the state of agriculture in both Caughnawaga and the St. Regis reserves is practically non-existent.
I think the ARDA approach would be helpful to both the Caughnawaga and St. Regis reserves, and I am told that somewhat similar situations exist on other reserves in southern Ontario. But I think we are fooling ourselves, and I do not really think this is the intention of the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), if we think that the problems on the Indian reserves of Canada can be solved within the reserves. In my view most Indian groups in this country look on their reserves as their cultural home, but I think the day has passed when there is much hope of any Indian group in this country developing their reserve as a self-sufficient region capable of supporting any substantial percentage of the tribal population.
The Indian tribes were just beginning to engage in agricultural development when Jacques Cartier landed at Montreal. Hoche-laga was one of the first Indian settlements in eastern Canada to combine hunting and fishing with a considerable agricultural development. The North American Indians were just beginning to settle down into an agricultural type of society. Some of the Indians in the western part of our country had also reached this stage. However, I do not believe that a very large degree of success in agriculture has ever been achieved on any Indian reserve in this country, with the exception of some in British Columbia. There are a number of very successful Indian farmers today in British Columbia but with the exception of that province I do not think agriculture has been much of a success on any Indian reserve in Canada.
There is no reason why this state of affairs should continue. There is no reason why a few farmers at least should not develop the existing land area available for farming on many of the southern Quebec and southern Ontario reserves. In my opinion, with the proper community help approach the ARDA program might very well be integrated into the more general program at present being advanced by the government which is designed to combine the social development and 20220-32

Mr. Speaker, in taking note of these petitions, as these citizens have a right that I should, I can simply say to them that this item has been placed by the government before the house as the first item of our parliamentary business following the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
My friend, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) in his remarks the other day ridiculed this petition and belittled this expression of views on so important a public project. I am not prepared to take so cavalier an attitude toward people who go to the trouble of setting down what they think and who are ready, on signing, also to pay toward the cost of the petition so their government and their parliament can know their views.
While I was in the locality last August I had several conversations with the people whom I met at the ferry, in the little village of Renata, for instance, and elsewhere along the way. The main impression I formed was that they wanted the uncertainty ended in order to be able to plan for the future and not continue living in doubt from day to day. I am confident that the arrangements now being made will work to their advantage.
It is not possible in a matter of this sort, involving as it does an agreement between three jurisdictions-two governments in Canada and the government of another country- to arrive at a settlement that can satisfy everyone. All that I can hope tc be able to

affirm to this house, is that with the help of my colleagues and my advisers we have reached a conclusion which we believe to be in the interests of Canada as well as in the interests of our neighbour and, of course, also in the interests of the province of British Columbia, the owner of the resource.
I have referred to the fact that there have been criticisms of the Columbia river treaty. Indeed it would be remarkable in a project of this magnitude and complexity if there had not. A vigorous and-

I think my hon. friend will find that nothing I said a couple of years ago is inconsistent with the conclusion I have been able to help to bring about.
The vigorous and frank exchange of views on issues of importance to the country as a whole has always been a feature of Canadian public life. In the case of this vitally important matter, the Columbia river treaty, the debate has had useful results where there was substance, merit and practical possibility to the ideas brought forward. As I have said, many of these points have been met in the protocol.
Over the past year I have had several meetings and extensive correspondence with all of the principal critics of the treaty in order that I might be fully familiar with their points of view. Our objective was to produce the best possible result, recognizing at the same time that the result had to be capable of agreement with the United States. The bargaining has been very hard indeed, and I am sure that the right hon. gentleman, the Leader of the Opposition, would agree with what I say. There were times when it looked as though all would collapse; times even when we began to think of how to phrase a press release that would explain why no agreement was possible.
But to have failed would have been a major defeat, a defeat, not just to the negotiators or to the governments but to the application of reason and common sense to the solution of human affairs. It takes two to agree-or in this case three-and all must benefit if agreement is to result.
I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that all parties to this treaty and to the protocol, do benefit and benefit greatly in the contemplated arrangements. I am convinced too that the best possible negotiable plan has been 20220-32i
Columbia River Treaty worked out, not simply in the interests of British Columbia but in the broad interest of Canada. We have here-I am convinced of it-sound provisions and sound protections to ensure the wise use of this great resource in our national interest over the years ahead.
Some critics still argue that the best sequence of projects has not been chosen. Not a single group of professional engineers that has made a detailed study of the projects says so-not one. No one had demonstrated that any other sequence would produce better results, having regard for all the considerations involved.
It has been argued that the storages should have been built at Dorr, Bull river and Luxor in the east Kootenay and upper Columbia valleys rather than at Libby. These projects would have flooded over six times as much land as Libby, and displaced well over a thousand more people. In addition, the projects which are primarily for the diversion of water from the Kootenay to the Columbia river, have not been proved economical on the basis of the power they produce in Canada. They would be the last storages to be constructed in any orderly development of the river basin in Canada, if in fact they ever did become economic. The Libby arrangement, on the other hand, as devised in the treaty, gives Canada an early and most economic source of additional power in the industrialized west Kootenay area in Canada. It also provides flood control protection to that area. It does this with a minimum flooding of Canadian land.
It has been argued that the Arrow lakes dam is of no value to Canada. That is simply not so. Not only does it produce benefits of a value almost twice the cost of the project but it is also the key to the operation of the vital Mica dam.

The hon. member asks: By whom? I am willing to tell him we have right here, in the service of the federal

Columbia River Treaty government, engineers who are, I believe, second to none. I have had an opportunity of conferring on this matter with people of engineering skill from the United States, British Columbia and other parts of Canada and, speaking for the federal government, I could name individuals whose devotion to the public service warrants the confidence that I have placed in them. Some of them are natives of British Columbia. Not only have we some of these engineers in the federal service, but there are individuals in the service of the government of British Columbia who have, by their long association with this project, and their engineering capacity, warranted our confidence in their skills pertinent to this particular matter.
The hon. gentleman seems to imply that we have relied on the engineering advice of people in another country. That is simply not the case-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
-and no one
knows it better than the hon. member who interrupts me at this very moment. I say, and I repeat what I have said, that it has been argued that the Arrow lakes dam is of no value to Canada. I say this is simply not so. Not only does it provide benefits which are almost twice the cost of the project, but it is the key to the operation of the vital Mica dam. Without high Arrow we could not enjoy both the great downstream benefits we are now assured of and the future possibilities of power development on the Columbia in Canada. That is the relation of the Arrow lakes project to the proposed dam at Mica.

The hon. gentleman makes happy interjections, and I have no quarrel with that. But I think he would agree with me that on a matter as important as this his interjections ought to be of such a character as would indicate he has a good appreciation of the problem.
It has been argued that we should not sell our downstream power benefits. Why not, if we have enough power in that part of Canada and will have surplus power for the years involved? To say we cannot terminate such a sale is nonsense and is not in conformity with either the treaty or the protocol.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext: What was the experience of Ontario?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
The water of the Columbia has flowed to the sea for thousands of years and it will continue to do so for thousands more, long after the hon. gentleman and I have left this house. The sensible

thing is to make the best possible arrangement to turn that flow to our advantage. For 30 years, the best arrangement is to sell the benefits.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext: And the jobs.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
There will still be benefits after 30 years and governments then, in their wisdom, can decide what is best to do. The right to full and unfettered control by Canada in the future has been amply protected in this treaty.
The situation which has been established is precisely the type contemplated by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in the address of October 2, 1961, from which I have already quoted. He said:
Before we permit the export of power or any natural resource-including power-we must be certain that there will be no shortage for our own national development in the foreseeable future.
At the same time we must realize that increased exports to the United States, and elsewhere, are a vital necessity for our progress and development. A "dog in the manger" attitude toward the export of any commodity, energy included, would in the long run harm us more than it would the United States.
The sale in question is not an export of energy. I have already dealt with that point. It is an export of a service. However, the basic conditions that would be required for an export of energy are met in this case.
It has been argued that we should not commit ourselves to provide flood control benefits after the term of the treaty, even if the United States needs them. Let us look at that argument.
I have already pointed out that the dams in Canada will be paid for 100 per cent in advance, with money left over. Part of the advance payment is $64,400,000 (U.S.) for flood control in the United States. After the period of the treaty we say that Canada will continue to provide flood control if it is needed, and we now have a voice in determining that need. That is one of the consequences of the protocol. If it is really needed, because a flood is coming in the valley, and if we provide flood control, the United States must pay us our operating costs and any and all economic loss we suffer as a result of doing it. In short, we are to use dams that are paid for, to provide a service we are paid for, in order to help a neighbour to avert or reduce a disaster. Would Canadians prefer to profit from our neighbour's grief? Would Canadians want to traffic in human suffering and loss? I am happy to say that neither the previous government of Canada nor this government, regard these as Canadian aspirations or as the basis on which our relations with the United States, or, indeed, with any other country, should be conducted.

Another criticism has been that there is not adequate protection for the possible diversion of water from the Columbia river to the prairies for consumptive purposes. I have had a lengthy correspondence on this point with the premier of Saskatchewan

a rather temperate dispute, Mr. Speaker. I find that the matter was raised with the previous government and that they, like me, could not find themselves in agreement with the premier's concern. Diversions for consumptive purposes are clearly contemplated under the treaty and the provision is made more specific in the protocol. However, diversion from the Columbia river basin to Saskatchewan is only a far-distant and remote possibility. I feel some doubt whether British Columbia would find it an agreeable project, especially when some of the diversions talked of would take some 30 per cent of the water away from the generators at Mica Creek. I feel, too, that annual costs of $7.50 to $10.50 per acre foot to put water from the Columbia basin into the South Saskatchewan, plus compensation for power losses in British Columbia, are not likely to be attractive when, to use figures supplied by Saskatchewan itself, water can be put in the same river from the North Saskatchewan for 40 cents; from the Athabasca for $3.50; from the Peace for $4.60; and even from the Fraser at lower cost-$6. We should have vision and imagination in resource use, but we should have some sense of proportion as well.
Let me say only two things at this time about any continuing criticism. In the first place, there seems to be no agreement among such critics as remain. The things desired by some are completely inconsistent with the things devoutly wished by others. Second, those who still criticize the arrangement on the ground of some imagined impairment of Canadian sovereignty really seem to have the matter upside down. If anybody has accepted dependence on anybody else, it is the United States which has become dependant on us and our storages. In fact, of course, neither of our countries is surrendering sovereignty. We are each entering, quite deliberately into an arrangement which will be, in the careful and conscientious judgment of each of us, to our own advantage. We would really be accepting a limitation on our sovereignty if we were to consider ourselves incapable of joining in such a beneficial arrangement.
In the months gone by the critics of the treaty have helped us-and I acknowledge this-by raising points that had to be provided for, points that were not thought of by the negotiators. I thank them for that. The treaty and the protocol are better for their efforts. But now the need is for action.
Columbia River Treaty
The Columbia river development plans have been worked on long enough-for 20 years. They have engaged the attention of two Canadian governments. They have engaged the attention of the government of the province of British Columbia. They have engaged the attention of the international joint commission and of special bodies designed to report to that commission. They have engaged the attention of qualified men and women selected by the government to pass upon studies made by government agencies.
So with this background of preparation I say that we have before this house a treaty that should, and will, commend itself to the members of this house, as I am sure it will to the great majority of the people of our country. The plans that have been prepared are good plans. The engineering is nearly finished. The money to be paid by the United States will be raised in the coming weeks. It is for us to decide whether the fruit of years of effort is to be gathered for the benefit of the people of Canada now and in the years to come. I have no doubt, on the basis of the record, what the verdict of this parliament will be.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it will be a matter of extreme satisfaction to very many thousands of people in the province of British Columbia that we have arrived at the point where the Columbia river treaty is to be submitted to the external affairs committee of this house for examination. It is no news to hon. members of this house, I imagine, that the possibility of the development of the Columbia, the contemplation of the harnessing of the resources of that great river, has occupied the attention and the dreams too of many British Columbians over many years-in fact, not just years but even generations.
It has always been believed that if once a means could be found by which the tremendous resources of that basin could be utilized for the generation of power to be added to the economic mainstream of the province, there would flow from such development immense benefits for every man, woman and child in the province, and beyond the province benefits to Canadians in many parts of the country. Now we are at the point where a specific proposition will be presented to parliament, a treaty that will permit the multiple-use development of the basin.
I was interested to listen to the minister's very comprehensive presentation of the background and the history of the negotiations, the history of the signing of the treaty, the development of the disagreement between the government of Canada and the government of British Columbia, the new agreement that has led to the protocol that is the additional

Columbia River Treaty document submitted to us in this house today. I was interested in the minister's speech for a good many reasons. The first one I am going to deal with can only be critical. I well remember during the period when negotiations were going on with the province of British Columbia, when the former Conservative government was dealing with the present government of British Columbia, there was not always in B.C. the most wholehearted approval of Conservative actions by those who now sit on the government side. In fact, by their words and actions I contend that they contributed to the breakdown in the relationship between the Conservative government of Canada and the government of British Columbia.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext: They made this an issue in two election campaigns, in 1962 and 1963; and they cannot escape that responsibility, because the things they said then are nowhere reflected in the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) in this house this afternoon and this evening.
