speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to dispose of this portion of my remarks first. I would like to make it plain that we in the opposition do not intend to obstruct or hinder the passage of the treaty through the committee, but we do reserve the right, and will use the right, to scrutinize all the terms of the agreement, particularly the protocol, with the greatest care. We too want to see this immense development take place in British Columbia. We have the right to expect that. After 13 years of roadblocking, from March of 1944 until the Conservative government came into power in 1957, no progress was made and the former Liberal administration had virtually to admit defeat in this regard. It was under the Conservative administration that the first agreements were reached with the province of British Columbia and the 50 per cent return of downstream benefits were secured from the United States. Therefore we are not interested in obstruction. But we also have suffered as a party. Our integrity has been attacked; our actions have been villified by the hon. gentlemen who sit opposite and like to pretend that what the minister has said today has represented their viewpoint throughout.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext: Hypocrites.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
On
February 28, 1963, one year ago, in the Van-
[Mr. Fleming (Okanagan-Revelstoke).l
couver Sun the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis), who is described in the article as having headed the Liberal party's committee on power and energy development during the last parliament, wrote an article under the general heading "The problems of power". The headline was, "The present Columbia river treaty ties Canada's hands". The first paragraph of this article written by the hon. gentleman who is now parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister reads:
The present Columbia river treaty is not good enough. It amounts to a sellout of our Canadian resources.
This embarrassing treaty must therefore be renegotiated-renegotiated in such a way as to make low cost power available to us as consumers in British Columbia.
But it was not renegotiated. There is not a single change of principle, nor was principle ever discussed in the protocol-

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext: Read the protocol.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
There is no change of principle in the protocol. The only principle change which was made was the agreement to sell all the downstream power benefits to the United States. Yet the principal consultant of the Liberal party said that it must be renegotiated in such a way as to make low cost power available to us as consumers in British Columbia. That is a repudiation of their whole position.
Then he said:
The U.S., which seeks flood control plus improved power development, could get early, major benefits by an altered schedule of works on the Canadian side.
There is not a single alteration in the schedule of work envisaged in the protocol. Then he said that under such new terms the Mica dam would be the best project with which to begin. The Mica dam is going to begin, as far as the engineering aspect makes it possible, simultaneously with both Duncan lake and high Arrow. Then the hon. member went on to say that there is no doubt that the present Columbia river treaty ties Canadian hands. He does not say in what fashion. Then he goes on to say:
It would flood thousands of acres of Canadian territory and it could prevent Canada from diverting the upper Kootenay into the Columbia and the Columbia into the Fraser river systems.
He was careful to say "could" because the treaty unrevised does provide for 1.5 million acres of diversion from the Kootenay river after 20 years. That was specifically written into the treaty and the protocol changes that in small measure, virtually in no effective manner at all. The hon. member goes on:
A good deal of scenery would be ruined and Canada might be obliged to hold back flood waters which would otherwise destroy property and endanger lives in the United States.

That is precisely what the treaty provided for. That is what the protocol provides for, and that is what would be necessary if we are to have a major development of a river in British Columbia. You could not develop a major river system of the size of the Columbia without changing the face of the land. To suggest as a criticism that thousands of acres of Canadian territory would be flooded is to suggest that this was a sufficiently bad thing to do away with the development.
Then the hon. member makes this suggestion:
We are obliged to build three storage dams costing around $400 million. The United States has to invest only $100 million in generating facilities and flood control payments to Canada. Yet the additional energy produced in the United States is split on a fifty-fifty basis.
The minister has just finished telling us that we do not want to take advantage of our friends' disadvantages. The United States has already spent $2 billion in developing the main stem of the Columbia and subsidiary rivers in the states of Washington and Oregon. Why would they be expected to spend an identical amount in the province of British Columbia at this stage of the development? It is as a consequence of the expenditure on that $2 billion development that there are already in existence downstream installations for us to derive power benefits from.
So it goes on, Mr. Speaker, and this was only one article; there were five in all. Hon. gentlemen opposite seem to find it amusing that I suggest that what the minister said this afternoon and this evening amounts to a repudiation of Liberal policy. What about developing the Columbia river in the first place? The hon. member for Coast-Capilano in his second article, which was published in the Vancouver Sun on March 1, 1963, said:
Other local hydro resources remain to be developed around Vancouver and in the vicinity of Trail. Operated in conjunction with existing facilities they could be added for three mills or less. We can obviously get by quite nicely until 1975. So we should be in no rush to build massive dams on the Peace, the Columbia, the Fraser, or any other major river

We have heard from the minister today that this view is rejected.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I will skip the third article, which mentions taxes, and I will come back to that a little later. I go to the fifth article, which deals with costs. The hon. member says:
Of course, our exports must be in surplus supply. They must be over and beyond our foreseeable requirements. Where there is the slightest doubt, these sales should not occur. And by all means let us keep our really low cost energy resources at home.
What has happened to this Liberal idea? First of all, we are going to sell power which
Columbia River Treaty we are told will be available at a cost of approximately 1.5 mills. That is the lowest cost power, I suspect, in the whole of Canada, let alone British Columbia, and we are going to sell all of it in the United States. Why? The minister has told us that British Columbia will have a surplus of power because of the Peace river development. You can get a surplus of power by building projects in all directions without regard to what it will cost. You can get a surplus of power very simply if you are not going to be bothered about what it costs to produce.
I think the people of British Columbia are entitled to know whether they are going to get this Peace river power, which is supposed to make these downstream benefits surplus, at the same cost as the downstream benefits. Or are they going to be asked to pay 10, 12 or 14 mills for it? We want to know on what basis the government of Canada agreed with the government of British Columbia that this power is surplus to requirements. We have already seen the statements of the premier of British Columbia, issued at approximately the time when the province decided to go ahead with the Peace river development, to the effect that there will be a "brown out" in the lower mainland before Peace river power could be delivered. Because it is going to take more than six years to develop the dam and before any power can be fed into the provincial electrical grid. If the premier is correct when he said that there would be a "brown out" in the industrial regions of the lower mainland before Peace river power could be produced, how can you justify, Mr. Speaker, the sale of all downstream power benefits to the United States in face of this possibility of shortage of low cost power to British Columbia industry? That we must know.
We do know that the power increment in British Columbia increases approximately 8 per cent annually, which is a compounding increase. We also know that there will be a tremendous demand for power in the province. We are capable of producing far more power, of course, than our requirements. But in this, five, six, or seven-year period-because it will be eight years before the Mica creek will be ready for the installation of generators, and six or seven years before the Peace river will be generating power-what is being done to assure British Columbia that the lowest cost energy, until these other projects are available, will be provided? And why have we agreed to allow these benefits to go to the United States when the United States already had agreed with the former government that, if low cost power from the downstream benefits was required in advance of the completion of any of the three storage projects, it could be drawn on and then later

Columbia River Treaty debited to our entitlement at a future time? These questions are questions which must be examined. They are questions which the house is entitled to have answered and which we feel the people of British Columbia must have answered.
Those of us in opposition have already been through a difficult period. The minister drew attention to the criticism which has arisen in some quarters of the treaty. We have gone through a great deal of trouble as a consequence of the criticism of hon. members opposite, as represented by these articles from which I have extracted quotations. We have been further criticized as well. After the Leader of the Opposition, when he was prime minister, made his announcement on March 19,	1962, at the federal-provincial
conference on long distance power transmission, and when the Conservative government's position on the export of power was enunciated, there was an opportunity for the renewal of negotiations with the province of British Columbia, and the negotiations had been renewed. What was the reaction of the Liberal opposition of that day? On May 14, 1962, in a statement made in Sherbrooke, Quebec, the leader of the opposition of that time said:
The existing treaty is not good enough. A responsible government could have made a better deal with the U.S.
A better deal can still be made. The only possible reason for a sudden settlement at this point is a desperate desire to preserve Social Credit and Conservative votes in B.C. For that purpose ratification of the treaty now in its present form would be sacrificing the best interests of Canada.
There is the statement of the Prime Minister on this matter. The leader of the Liberal party in British Columbia on September 28 in a statement made at Victoria said:
The total and abject surrender of Prime Minister Diefenbaker and his cabinet ministers to the government of British Columbia and to Mr. Bennett on this issue of long term export of hydro power and the question of the Columbia river treaty is designed only to win the support of 30 Social Credit members.
The minister did not have to sell these downstream benefits to get the support of the Social Credit members in this house. If the reason for agreeing to the downstream disposal of power is the same as they suggested the Conservatives' reason would have been, it was a wasted effort. As the Conservative government throughout the negotiation with the government of British Columbia made very plain, we would not oppose the export of surplus power but it would have to be proved surplus to the requirements of the province and this was set forward at that conference to which I have referred, the federal-provincial conference on long distance

power transmission of March 19, 1962. At that time the prime minister, now Leader of the Opposition, said:
In December the government on the recommendation of the national energy board approved a number of power export licences. When a new block of power is brought into an original system, export of the surplus portion may be desirable or even necessary if the development itself is to be feasible, but the export should be confined to power that the national energy board is prepared to certify as surplus to Canada's requirements now and for the foreseeable future.
We do not argue with the export of surplus power but we do demand to know how it can be considered surplus and we come back again to the minister's statement on the Peace river. Certainly if the Peace river supplies the great load of power that it is supposed to provide for the province it is going to have not only power from that source, but further development of the Columbia will no doubt create a surplus that can be exported or, as we hope be fed into a national grid system to provide power to provinces without adequate supply at the present time, or not likely to have adequate supplies in the future.
We do not argue against export but we do feel that this downstream power, or the sale of it should have been considered by the national energy board. The minister contends that that power is not export, that it is generated in the United States, therefore it can be sold in the United States and need not be considered in terms of export. Now that power is generated by American installations only as a consequence of construction of Canadian works on the Columbia river. It is power created in fact by Canadian installations, because it would not be created without the Canadian installations and in that sense at least it may be considered an export. Certainly it is the property of the province of British Columbia, and I do feel that we must be told either here in the house before this debate concludes, or in committee, on what basis the decision was made to sell all the downstream benefits downstream, and what guarantee the government secured from the province of British Columbia that equivalent low cost power could be provided to the people and industries of British Columbia.

speechtext: Is the hon. member aware that the dominion bureau of statistics has published a forcecast of a surplus, a substantial surplus of power in British Columbia over the next five years?

speechtext:
I have had statistics provided to me in the past by the hon. member who is now the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) and if I were going to deal in statistics I am sure I could supply the hon. member with many that may come from equally reliable sources, and I could prove a great many points; but he has managed to overlook once again the essential point and obscures the situation, as the minister was doing. I know there could be a surplus. I know there will be a surplus. Is the Peace river power as low cost as the surplus we are going to sell? We could all instal Delco plants and make power in our backyards, but would it be economic? What we want to know is whether this power that is retained in the province to drive the wheels of industry and to light and heat the homes of the people, is as cheap as the power we are selling in the United States.
Somewhere in one of these articles I have referred to earlier the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) has said our hands were tied, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs said this protocol that he has negotiated has given us greater freedom of action and movement and so on particularly with respect to diversion.
I would like to draw your attention to the statement made by the right hon. the prime minister of the former government at the time of the signing of the treaty. He said: The treaty makes provision for a number of diversions of water that may be made by Canada from the Kootenay river in its natural course in different circumstances and at different times. It will be possible, even if the United States exercises its option to build the Libby dam, to divert 1.5 million acre feet of water per year from the Kootenay river in Canada into the head waters of the Columbia river to increase power production in Canada. It will not be advantageous to do this until generators have been installed on our part of the Columbia, which will not be for some years. This right is exercisable by Canada at any time after 20 years from the ratification date. If the United States does not exercise its option to build Libby dam, the treaty provides that Canada has the immediate right to make a major diversion from the Kootenay river into the Columbia river that would send approximately 90 per cent of the
Columbia River Treaty flow down that course. There are also provisions for major diversions at the end of 60 and 80 years even if the United States has built the Libby dam. The permanent rights of Canada to the free use of the waters of the Kootenay river are thus protected.
To suggest, as the minister did suggest today, that the diversionary rights of Canada on the waters of the Kootenay were not protected by the treaty is not correct. This definition of what was contained in the treaty was clearly explained at the time of the treaty.
We can look at this protocol and note the summary that is contained in page 126 of the green book we were provided with during the past week. If hon. members seem to feel when I suggested there had been no negotiation of new principles that was an unreasonable statement, let us look at the summary here. There are new procedures, no new principles. The summary states, "Reconfirmation in positive terms of Canada's right to make diversion." You will note it says reconfirmation, not renegotiation-confirmation is all. The summary further states "Clarification of Canada's rights to continue in perpetuity any diversion to the Kootenay river in accordance with the treaty". Again you will note it says clarification, not new negotiation, not new principles. Further from the summary: "Confirmation of Canadian control of the detailed operation of storage for power purposes". It says confirmation, not renegotiation. It is confirmation of something that already existed in the other treaty. And so it goes. We have in fact had a very strong presentation by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He spoke well of the role played by Hon. Davie Fulton as head of the negotiating committee. I know that the work done by Mr. Fulton was looked upon by him with respect and regard as it was by a great many people in British Columbia, certainly by many in this party and by myself personally.
One of the things I had discussed with Mr. Fulton on a previous occasion and which I brought up in the house during the throne speech of May of last year was the question of whether it was possible to examine the development on the Columbia river as it is now projected and to have a look at the storage behind Mica creek to see if it is not possible that the dam can be built 15 feet higher than was contemplated in the original treaty as a consequence of a reassessment of costs. Here again there would be no necessity for changing the principle but it would be possible in the reconsideration of costs of the structure to make provision so that substantially greater storage can take place behind that dam and in that reservoir than had been contemplated.

If this is so, is it economically feasible? Could it be that a degree of the storage from the high Arrow project could be transferred to storaee behind Mica creek? If this additional height can be built within present cost estimates, if this water can be transferred, is it economically sound to suggest that part of the Arrow lake storage can be transferred to that reservoir? If so, it would be possible to eliminate a substantial amount of the criticism in British Columbia that now exists with regard to the treaty and the protocol because it would preserve some of the lands that are now likely to be flooded.
That is one idea. Also, in the course of his discussions with the province of British Columbia has the minister satisfied himself that the province has committed the development of the Columbia to an authority that will take into account all possibilities of development and not concern itself exclusively with power production and storages only? I ask this question because in British Columbia we know that the B.C. hydro and power authority has been charged with the responsibility of developing the river, but many of us feel the province should be designating a body with far greater authority and far greater terms of reference, something in the nature of the Tennessee valley authority under which recreation, conservation of wildlife and fish, conservation of forests and land and the redevelopment of beaches and recreational areas around the lakes and storages that may be created in time will be taken care of, a proper authority to consider compensation for and relocation of people who will be displaced by flooding, an authority that will take into account the tremendous impact on the towns in the Columbia river valley which will be affected by flooding, some of which will actually have essential public facilities such as sewage and water interfered with by the rising of the waters in the lakes and the river. There is also the matter of the impact of the tremendous influx of workmen and their families on these small towns which will have to provide housing, schools, medical services and so on for these people. What provision has been made for these things?
I realize at once that it is not the responsibility of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) nor does it come within the jurisdiction of the government of Canada, but I do feel that these considerations must be provided for. We have had no reassurance from any source yet that all of the aspects of this development have been taken into account or that the hydro and power authority of British Columbia has even been given the opportunity to provide for this sort of development. This is the sort of
[Mr. Fleming (Okanagan-Revelstoke) .1

thing with regard to which I feel the federal government must at least use its influence in negotiations to be sure that wildlife, fisheries, recreation, forestry and all these other requirements, as well as human needs are being met. While I listened with interest to the statement made by Mr. Keenleyside, the co-chairman of the hydro and power authority, which the minister read and which I had also read myself, I am afraid it does not seem to go far enough because he says that hydro is not a soulless engineering machine and that it will deal generously and sympathetically with each person who has to move his home or his business. The problem is far greater because the economy of our towns and villages will be affected. The face of the land will be changed, and consequently the authority that does have the responsibility for this development in British Columbia must have a far wider objective than simply creating dams, controlling the flow of water and installing generators.
Finally, it is desirable to emphasize once again that if the treaty projects represent the whole of the Columbia development, then the development should not take place, but if they represent the beginning of the Columbia development and provide a foundation for the installation of generators at Mica creek and the building in time of dams at Murphy creek, Downey creek and Revelstoke canyon and subsidiary dams on the Kootenay between Nelson and Castlegar and possibly other installations in Kootenay east, if these things follow then the development of the Columbia is, as the minister said, a great achievement for Canada. But if it is no more than the building of these storages and one dam capable of producing power, then it is not justified. We must have the absolute assurance of British Columbia-I guess we had better have that in writing too-that the province intends to proceed with the full development of the river and thus provide the people of British Columbia with an immense opportunity, and also provide for Canada opportunities for employment and production in many of our great eastern factories, opportunities that are so great it is almost impossible even now to realize their full potential.

I think it was conceived in avarice and born in apathy, and I do not think that the protocol has done anything to remove the worst features of the treaty. The previous speaker was quite correct when he said that the only fundamental change which the protocol has brought about is that the downstream benefits are now being sold for a lump sum paid in advance. That is the only change. As someone has said, this treaty is very much like an old hag putting on lipstick and rouge, not so much to enhance her beauty but to hide her ugliness.
I was interested in hearing the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) say this afternoon that the Columbia river treaty which was signed on January 17, 1961 was a credit to the administration of that time and that he had been engaged in the task merely of making a good treaty a better treaty. Well, Mr. Speaker, that is not what his colleagues were saying in 1961, 1962 and 1963. It is not what the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) and the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) were telling the people of British Columbia in the last two federal elections. In those elections people were being told that this constituted a sell-out, that this was the export of jobs, and that this was a betrayal to the interests of the United States.
Now, overnight, it has become a good treaty, a treaty, according to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, that was a credit to the government which signed it in January, 1961. It seems that as hon. members climb the ladder of political success the altitude has an amazing effect upon their convictions and their points of view.
There is no argument about the case which the Secretary of State for External Affairs put forth about the tremendous potential of the Columbia river, and what it can do to increase the well-being and raise the living standards of the people of B.C. and of the northwestern states of the United States. No one is quarrelling for a moment with the idea of developing the Columbia river basin. This is a great natural resource which can serve mankind for generations to come.
What we as parliamentarians have to be concerned about is whether or not this treaty is in the best interests of the Canadian people, whether this is like the chicken pie-one chicken and one horse; whether all the benefits are on one side, or whether it has been
Columbia River Treaty negotiated in such a way that the interests of the Canadian people have been safeguarded.
I ask the house to take a look first of all at what Canada will get out of this treaty. The treaty, and now the protocol, stipulate that we will get for our downstream benefits, sold in bulk, on October 1, 1964, $274.8 million in Canadian funds. Then we will get for flood control payments a total of $69.6 million, $12 million for the Duncan dam when it is completed in 1968, $56.3 million for the Arrow dam when it is completed in 1969, and $1.3 million for the Mica dam when it is completed in 1973. This will make a grand total of $344.4 million.
Then the minister, in his press releases, did some sleight of hand by which he said that by the year 1973, if you got interest on this money, it would be worth $501 million. Of course the fact is that most of this money will be spent before 1973.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext: It is still valuable.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
The most important consideration is, what will this amount of money buy? It will take this $344.4 million to build the three dams and, if the engineering estimates are accurate, there will be $53.4 million left over. Personally I do not think there will be much left over. Most people's experience with engineering estimates is usually that actual costs are higher than estimates, and I doubt very much if there will be anything left. But assuming the figures are accurate, and there are $53.4 million left over, the minister's own press release says that this $53 million will pay half the generating installations on Mica creek, and that will have a value to the power users in B.C. of $16 million a year from 1973 to the year 2003.
In the first place, Mr. Speaker, that will be more than offset if the Peace river power costs just one mill more than the power from the Columbia river; but even if we get $16 million a year of benefit, that will not begin to compensate Canada for the payments that will have to be made, to people who are dispossessed from their homes and places of business, for communities that are flooded, to say nothing of the fact that it will not begin to pay for the loss of the productivity of thousands of acres of land which will be flooded in perpetuity.
The $69.6 million which we are getting for flood control means that we are to supply 15J million acre feet of storage, most of it productive land, timber and agricultural land. All this will be taken out of production in perpetuity for $69.6 million.
This afternoon the Secretary of State for External Affairs made a great point of the fact that the federal government was not being

Columbia River Treaty called upon now to make any federal contribution. Of course it is not, because what the government of Canada has done is to sell the downstream benefits for a lump sum, and that sum will do little more than pay for the construction of three dams whose primary purpose is flood control in the United States, and to increase power production in the United States.
What does the United States get out of this treaty and protocol? First of all they get flood control that it has been estimated in some quarters is worth some $500 million. Certainly Mr. Stewart Udall, the secretary of the interior, set the value of power and flood control at $710 million if the United States had to undertake it alone. He said about $150 million was for generating installation, which means that this flood control is worth over $500 million to the United States. The United States is now getting this by paying us $69.6 million.
The second thing she gets is greatly increased generating power that would cost her a great deal of money if she had to produce it in the United States.
I have here a copy of an address which was delivered to the association of professional engineers of Alberta, in Calgary, on Saturday, March 23, 1963 by General A. G. L. McNaughton, and in the course of that speech this is what he said:
The studies in the international joint commission and elsewhere have shown that the benefits to stream flow control which Canada can provide to the United States are so large that to match them within their own territory the United States would need to expend close to a billion dollars even if they could obtain permission to use the sites for the works required.
We sometimes speak of the Americans and ourselves having divided these downstream benefits on a fifty-fifty basis, but as General McNaughton said in his address to the professional engineers in Alberta the formula the Americans have used has resulted in their getting 60 per cent of the downstream benefits, whereas Canada is only getting 40 per cent, and the Americans' own published figures will substantiate that statement.
When, this afternoon, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) quoted the Prime Minister as having said in a speech in Vancouver that it was folly to spend large sums of money just to provide cheap power to the United States, I wonder what he thinks this treaty and protocol are doing? This is providing cheap power to the United States. All the United States is paying for is the downstream benefits in advance, and less than $70 million for flood control.
A third thing which the Americans get out of this treaty is complete control of the Columbia river basin. A great deal has been

said about the protocol but I ask the house to take a look at annex A of the treaty, and to look at clause 7. Clause 7 makes the situation very clear. It says:
After at-site power is developed at the site referred to in paragraph 5(a) or power generating facilities are placed in operation in Canada downstream from that site, the storage operation will be changed so as to be operated in accordance with operating plans designed to achieve optimum power generation at-site in Canada and downstream in Canada and the United States of America, including consideration of any agreed electrical co-ordination between the two countries.
Here is, really, the nub of the whole question-this matter of optimum power generation. I do not think I could do better, in trying to clarify exactly what is meant by this, than to refer to an article which appeared in the International Journal volume 18, number 2. I wish to read from an article written by General A. G. L. McNaughton in which he explains what optimum power generation means for Canada.

speechtext:
The hon. member for-is it Rosedale?-keeps trying to be witty and only half succeeds. This is what General McNaughton has to say in this article at page 158 of the International Journal:
Later on, when Canadian at-site generation comes to be installed, an even more unfortunate arrangement develops its adverse effect to cut down drastically the possibilities for production of power for the Canadian load. This derives from clause 3 of the preamble, which I have mentioned previously, and which defines the intent of the parties to the treaty as: "being desirous of achieving the development of the resources in a manner that will make the largest contribution to the economic progress of both countries and the welfare of their peoples of which these resources are capable."
These are the general's comments. He continues:
This is collective. It means that the regulation of flow from the Canadian reservoirs must he directed in making the largest contribution, to provide both in kind and amount the greatest possible total benefit in the basin. This is a perfectly laudable objective, no doubt, in integrated operations for one country, but when the result is "peaking power" to meet the larger U.S. interest while Canada requires "firm power", there is a clash of interest in which Canada as the smaller will suffer very seriously through the results of the objective of regulation specified in Annex A, paragraph 7.
That is the one I have quoted. The article goes on:
This calls for "operating plans designed to achieve optimum generation at-site in Canada and the United States" including-as a later stage-

"consideration of any agreed electrical co-ordination between the two countries". Basin "optimum" is largely the kind of regulation which the United States wants, not what Canada needs.
If one looks at clause 5 of annex A he begins to realize the tremendous control which this treaty will place in the hands of the United States. The clause says:
For flood control operation, the United States entity will submit flood control operating plans which may consist of or include flood control storage reservation diagrams and associated criteria for each of the dams. The Canadian entity will operate in accordance with these diagrams or any variation which the entities agree will not derogate from the desired aim of the flood control plan.
The latter part of the paragraph says:
After consultation with the Canadian entity the United States entity may from time to time as conditions warrant adjust these storage reservation diagrams within the general limitations of flood control operation. Evacuation of the storages listed hereunder will be guided by the flood control storage reservation diagrams and refill will be as requested by the United States entity after the consultation with the Canadian entity.
That is abundantly clear. There will be consultation, but the final decision with regard to this flow will lie entirely in the hands of the United States authorities.
Contrast that position with the agreement made in the case of the only dam which is to be constructed in the United States, the Libby dam, which will be built in Montana. Here, the story is different. Under the terms of article XII-and I shall read clause (5)- it is provided:
If a variation in the operation of the storage is considered by Canada to be of advantage to it the United States of America shall, upon request, consult with Canada. If the United States of America determines that the variation would not be to its disadvantage it shall vary the operation accordingly.
Surely, that is crystal clear. The Libby dam in the United States will be controlled by the United States. If it is not to its disadvantage, it shall vary the operation. But if it feels it would be to its disadvantage, then it does not have to vary the operation. This is why it is so completely meaningless to talk about the control we are going to have of the Kootenay. As I say, the Libby dam in the United States will be controlled by the United States, and the dams built in Canada will also be controlled by the United States. This is certainly a one-sided agreement.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs said this afternoon that the diversion from the Kootenay into the Columbia had been clarified by the protocol. This, again, is a matter of giving a legal right which has little or no value because since the Americans are the upstream nation in the case of the Kootenay, and since they will be operating a dam at the Libby, they will have the right to determine how much water would come into
Columbia River Treaty Canada, how much water would be available for development in west Kootenay, how much water would be available for power generation and, in addition, when we would get it, if at all. May I also point out that in spite of the protocol, article XIII of the treaty, in subsections (2) and (3) makes it perfectly clear that we cannot divert water until after 20 years have passed, and then only 1,500,000 acre feet out of a total of five million acre feet.
But the most important thing the United States will get out of this treaty is tremendous quantities of water, and water at flow rates dictated by the needs of the United States. The Americans have been 40 or 50 years ahead of us in recognizing that the day will come on this continent when water will be more important than gold. That is why the United States have spent the last 30 years impounding water. That is why the United States today pipes water hundreds of miles down into states like California, because the Americans know that unless you have quantities of water you cannot have agriculture, you cannot have industry and you cannot have large urban centres. I do not think the Americans are worried about the power. I think they are worried about flood control; but what they are primarily concerned about is to control a great volume of water, and this is what we are giving them by turning over to them the resources of the fourth largest river on this north American continent. And we are doing it, I may say, for a measly $344.4 million which is going to be used to build storage dams primarily to help the United States.

British Columbia, of course, would have to be compensated for this, but it would have to be a multiple-purpose project. In great areas like the prairies the only way you can supply water is if it is used for power, for irrigation, for domestic consumption, for industry or for recreation. That is the only way the South Saskatchewan system could have been built. It would not have stood alone on any one of those uses, but when it is a multipurpose project it is possible for it to be economic. When the minister says that we have the legal right to divert waters to the prairies for irrigation, I want to point out that we may have the legal right but it is a meaningless right, because it would be uneconomic unless this water could be used for electrical energy as well as for irrigation and other uses.
The minister says that it is doubtful whether British Columbia would want to part with this water. I suggest that the day may come when the province of British Columbia will be glad to sell 10 per cent of the flow of the Columbia river, not only because of the revenue it would derive, but because the more people there are, the more products which are grown, and the greater is the development on the prairies, the greater will be the prosperity of British Columbia, which is the port for Alberta and the western half of the province of Saskatchewan.

We are not asking to have both sides. We are saying that we have complete control over a river which rises in Canada, a river over which we have complete control under the boundary water treaty act of 1909. We ought to co-operate with the United States so far as flood control is concerned. But the primary purpose of developing the resources of the Columbia river basin should be for the benefit of Canadians, and I suggest that that is not what this treaty provides. I believe that in this treaty the sharp Yankee traders took our naive and inexperienced Canadian negotiators into the camp and took them for "suckers".
I ask this house, Mr. Speaker, to remember that these resources do not belong to us. We merely hold them in trust for future generations of Canadians who will live in this country for all time. I say to the house that this treaty and this protocol means that we are selling our birthright for a mess of pottage, largely to satisfy the vanity of a provincial premier and to meet the needs of a power-hungry and water-hungry neighbour to the south.
I should like to remind this house that over 50 years ago the republic of Panama signed an agreement with the United States regarding a canal and the supply of water for that canal. At the present time it takes something in the neighbourhood of 1,000 million gallons a year to supply the Panama canal. As a result of that treaty the Panamanians now find they have not sufficient water for their own needs. This is why there is trouble in Panama. This is why the signs say "Go home Yankee". I want to tell the house that if we are so forgetful of our duty as to ratify this treaty, the day will come in Canada when generations not very far distant from today will curse the day that the parliament of Canada gave away this great heritage of the Canadian people.
I am glad that this treaty and the protocol are going to be referred to the committee on external affairs. This is a step which we urged on the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson)

We shall urge the members of that committee to hear all points of view and to allow prominent engineers who have expressed their misgivings about this treaty to appear and give evidence. I hope the committee, after it has investigated this matter, will recommend to parliament and the government that this matter be held in abeyance until the treaty can be renegotiated along the lines of the proposals set forth in the so-called McNaughton plan, so that the mobilization of the Columbia river basin resources will be predicated on the interests of the people of Canada to a degree which is not present in the treaty.
If the committee brings back this treaty and recommends its ratification, we in the New Democratic party will oppose its ratification, and will do everything in our power to prevent this parliament giving its assent to what we consider a great betrayal of the interests of the people of British Columbia in particular, and of the people of Canada in general. We feel that unless we register our objection we will not be true to our convictions, and we will not be keeping faith with future generations of Canadians.

speechtext: As there is not unanimous consent I will call on the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson).

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have listened to the various contributions to this debate, which is concerned with one of the most important pieces of legislation before the house in this session, with much interest. I have a very personal interest in this matter because as I stand at the most westerly point of my electoral district I can see the headwaters of the Columbia running to the west and to the south, the headwaters of the Athabaska running to the north, and the headwaters of the Saskatchewan river system running to the east. Anyone who has had this experience can understand the tremendous resources which are


ours in Canada as far as precious life-giving water is concerned.
I maintain it will be a very cold day in June indeed before western Canada is short of water. I very much welcome the speed with which the government has placed before us this important matter of the ratification of the new protocol to the Columbia river treaty. Contrary to the hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), I feel that it is a thoroughly good treaty, and rather than being a decorated old hag it is in my opinion a wild horse that has been running without control for many years through the valleys of the Rocky mountains, and it is now being brought under control to plow a mighty furrow for Canada in the development of its industry and commerce.
This is one of the most far reaching projects for the development of the natural resources of Canada that we have yet seen and the benefits that it can bring not only to British Columbia but to the entire nation of Canada are of such a magnitude that we who stand here at this point today cannot really fully understand. For this reason it is not our intention to enter into any lengthy debate at this time, and it is our intention at this point not to take any further part in the debate on the resolution stage.
I believe it is essential that this treaty and the protocol be brought before the external affairs committee at the earliest possible time, when we can hear the experts and when we can argue and discuss the details to our hearts' content. I believe at this point as well that it is right that we should pay tribute to the premier of British Columbia who, since his first election to power in 1952, has doggedly and in the face of many discouragements persisted in going forward with the development of this immense concept, and to whose credit must be laid many of the features that have gone into the making of this agreement, the price at which the power has been sold; the two rivers policy that has placed Canada in such a favourable bargaining position; the whole concept of downstream benefits and the ingenious and profitable manner of making payment incorporated in the protocol, whereby Canada will in effect be receiving the construction of her part of the project virtually free of charge.
I was much impressed by the remarks of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) today as he gave us a few of the statistics which relate to the project itself. The Columbia river project has a hydroelectric potential of some 145 billion kilowatt hours at its mean flow. This is greater than any other river in North America and it represents 15 per cent of the existing water

power in the entire world. Not only are billions of dollars involved in the Columbia itself, but the national policies of both countries regarding water, including flow control and power development of rivers that cross the international border, will be established by this treaty.
I believe that it is good for us while we listen to the negative aspects of this debate to remind ourselves of the positive side that the project represents. I have before me a document which probably most of the members of this house have in their possession. It is a statement on the Columbia river agreement by Dr. H. L. Keenleyside, chairman of the British Columbia hydro power authority, a man of no mean background and experience. He states briefly that:
Canada has undertaken to ensure that British Columbia will build three major dams on the Columbia river, and to use them to regulate the flow of water into the United States in accordance with an agreed plan of operation for a period of 30 years. For that time United States will have the use of the Canadian half as well as its own half of the extra power generated in the United States plants. Canada also agreed that the United States may build a dam at Libby on the Kootenai river in Montana in spite of the fact that this will flood some 40 miles of the southern Kootenay valley in British Columbia.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has said that the McNaughton plan will flood less of Canadian soil than the present plan calls for. I think it would be well if he would examine his facts because it will actually flood three times as much.

speechtext: Not at all.

speechtext:
In return for these services the United States will pay to Canada and Canada will instantly transfer to British Columbia the sum of $274.8 million on October 1,	1964 and an additional total
amount of $69.6 million will be paid in 1968, 1969 and 1973 as three Canadian dams come into operation at Duncan, Arrow and Mica.
I did not really intend to enter into too much of the controversy of this debate but again I find my hon. colleague from Burnaby-Coquitlam says that Duncan lake dam and Libby dam would not yield any power benefits for Canada. I do not quite understand this. The Duncan lake dam will have at-sit.e generation and the Libby adds about one third more generation to the west Kootenay plants in Canada. Let us keep our statistics straight when we come to criticize this treaty.
Dr. Keenleyside goes on to say this about the specific advantages:
What advantages will these payments bring to Canada and to British Columbia? They can be quickly summarized:
It is good for us to remind ourselves of them.
Columbia River Treaty
The total amount received from the United States will pay all the capital costs of the storage dams as they occur. It will pay about half the capital costs of the generators at Mica. It will enable a 1.8 million kilowatt generator installation at Mica to produce 6.6 billion kilowatt hours of energy annually for less than 1.5 mills per kilowatt hour.
The hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. Fleming) wonders what the at-site generation price is going to be for this power. Here it is. He wonders what responsibility the government of British Columbia will have for its own citizens that are affected under this development. I assure him that from their past record they will take care of the citizens of British Columbia very well as they have been doing for the last dozen years or more.
The corresponding cost under development without the treaty would be nearly four mills per kilowatt hour. The savings at Mica at full production will be about $16 million a year.
What more evidence does he need? The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam says that the cost of such projects always runs more than the actual engineering estimates. It is interesting to note that right now the Peace river development is $33 million under the estimates to date.
Going on with Dr. Keenleyside's statement, he says:
An alternative way of stating the advantages accruing to Canada and to British Columbia would be to say that the United States payments would during the 30 year periods of sale (i) pay off all the capital costs of the dams and reservoirs at Duncan, Arrow and Mica, (ii) pay all the operating expenses of these storage projects and (iii) leave a surplus of approximately $40 million at the end of the sales contract period.
The arrangements ensure that the storage projects in Canada will be debt free as they are constructed. This compares with a normal amortization period for such projects of 50 to 100 years.
Construction of the treaty projects on this basis with all costs paid will make possible enormous economic advantages to Canada and British Columbia which could only be attained, if at all, at much higher cost through development without the treaty.
These advantages make possible a number of very important features:
The installation of over 4 million kilowatts at points on the Columbia river in Canada which will produce energy at a cost of about 2 mills per kilowatt hour.
This is what power is going to cost. Where can you get it cheaper than that? The installed capacity will be more than 1J times the total present hydroelectric installation in British Columbia and about 20 per cent of what it is in all of Canada.
Reduction in the B.C. hydro system cost of generation from just over 5 mills today to approximately 21 mills by the time the Columbia river in Canada is fully developed.

Columbia River Treaty
Who is this going to help? Right now the prospect for the development of industry-in the interior of British Columbia is so overwhelming that it cannot really be seen at this point. This is simply because of the prospect of cheap power which we have to have if we are going to attract industry and which will have untold benefits for every part of Canada, not just the area concerned. Dr. Keenleyside goes on to mention other advantages.
Delivery of this power to centres throughout the southern half of the province at about 3 mills per kilowatt hour.
Where can you get power for that price any other place in Canada or in the world?
Prevention of floods in settled areas on the Kootenay and Columbia rivers in Canada.
Eeceipt at the end of the 30 year contract of payments from the still continuing downstream benefits of from $5 to $10 million annually.
Additional payments of up to $8 million by the United States for extra flood control if it is required during the treaty period as well as special flood control compensation for any emergency requirements of the United States during and after the life of the treaty.
Permit the creation of a Columbia-Peace high voltage transmission network that will bring the full resources of the two great rivers within reach of all major communities in the province.
We could go on and elaborate in detail the tremendous benefits that will come from the development of this important project involved in this treaty. I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that never in Canada have we had such prospects before us in relation to the development of our natural resources and the provision of employment and opportunities for the citizens of Canada. If we had more of this in Canada we would double our gross national product every 10 years, our population every 20 years and the unemployment we have with us now would melt away like the snows are melting in the spring weather we have been having in Ottawa during the last few days.
It is my contention, Mr. Speaker, that we have a tremendous opportunity to serve not only Canadian citizens of our day but those of generations to come as a result of this project. I would also remind hon. members that the United States does not have to have this. The waters that have been referred to today as being so precious have been running down into the Pacific ocean since the days of creation and they will continue to do so as long as the rains fall, unless we use our heads and permit the development of a project such as we have before us at the present time.
Within a few years the United States will be able to produce atomic power at rates that will be comparable to the cost of normal hydroelectric power today. If we are not

careful we will lose the whole opportunity that this treaty brings to us and all its advantages to Canada.
I am pleased that the government has shown such dispatch in concluding the negotiations and bringing these measures before us. This certainly represents quite a change from the rather less enthusiastic approach to the issue which resulted in the dragging out of negotiations fruitlessly for so many years before 1952 and then again after 1958.
It has been said that the people of British Columbia are opposed to this project. It was interesting to hear of the petition that was brought to our attention this afternoon, but I have a letter here from the Nelson chamber of commerce. Nelson is right in the heart of this project area and the people there know the benefits that can be realized. The letter is dated January 16, 1964. Listen to what it says:
We in the Kootenays needs this development. We are very serious when we say this...We in this area know full well that the development of the Columbia river will do much to boost the economy and give the very much needed employment, besides benefitting the whole country.
Our chamber of commerce Columbia river treaty committee, chaired by an engineer and with a picked committee, professional and others, studied the treaty word by word, spent many weeks on this, and were unanimously in favour of its ratification and the selling of the power.
On April 3, 1963 the same chamber of commerce unanimously passed a resolution at a special general meeting, and it reads in part as follows:
Therefore be it resolved that the Nelson chamber of commerce support the Columbia river treaty plan and the agreement be ratified at the earliest possible date.

The opposition too, of
course, has declared itself in favour of the treaty, for essentially it is only an improvement on what was agreed to two years ago under the previous administration.

speechtext: What is the improvement?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL

Approximately $100 million. What was so advantageous to Canada then can hardly be less so with the improvements that have been made in the treaty since that date. We know that the prime minister of Canada of that day, the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) issued a press release following the signing of the Columbia river treaty in Washington on January 17, 1961. That release read in part as follows:
So far as Canada Is concerned, the most important single feature of the treaty is the one I have already referred to-the recognition of the principle of division of downstream benefits. From that

principle all the great advantages that are possible for Canada as a result of co-operative development of the Columbia basin flow. Without that principle the entire arrangement would be fruitless for this country. Our predecessors in office had failed to achieve recognition of this basic point. We have succeeded. The treaty embodies the principle that downstream benefits are to be divided equally. That alone is a success of the most outstanding character.
We have been able to achieve this in a way which will fully respect the sovereignty of each country. By avoiding any complicated cost-sharing and by making the arrangement as self-enforcing as possible we have ensured that there will be no unnecessary intrusion into each others affairs across the international boundary.
Thus has spoken that great self-named champion of Canadian sovereignty, and I cannot quite understand how there can be any opposition from the Conservative party at this time that can make any more sense than to criticize the Liberals for something they failed to do. The time is drawing near to ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker. May I call it ten o'clock?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is the intention of the government that the order already announced should be followed. This debate will continue and after the end of the debate on the resolution now before us we will be taking in order the motions for the establishment of special committees of the house. After that we will be taking the electoral boundaries readjustment bill.
